3. Vanishing cycles and Coxeter–Dynkin diagrams
For isolated hypersurface singularities, nearby smooth fibers contain vanishing cycles. Their intersection matrix can be encoded as a graph called a Coxeter–Dynkin diagram.
A paper on distinguished bases of singularities says the intersection matrix of a distinguished basis of vanishing cycles is encoded by a Coxeter–Dynkin diagram of the singularity. sciencedirect.com
So here the graph records how cycles collide or interact as you approach the singular point:
singularity→Milnor fiber→vanishing cycles→intersection graph\text{singularity}

\text{intersection graph}singularity→Milnor fiber→vanishing cycles→intersection graph
This is especially close to your catastrophe/monodromy intuition.
4. McKay correspondence: quotient singularities become graphs
For quotient singularities of the form:
C2/Γ\mathbb{C}^2 / \GammaC2/Γ
where Γ\GammaΓ is a finite subgroup of SL2(C)SL_2(\mathbb{C})SL2​(C), the singularity is linked to an ADE Dynkin diagram. In the McKay correspondence, the representation graph of Γ\GammaΓ matches the resolution graph of the singularity. A lecture source states that the exceptional divisor of the minimal resolution of C2/Γ\mathbb{C}^2/\GammaC2/Γ is a tree of rational curves in an ADE Dynkin diagram configuration. Freemath
So:
finite group→McKay graph→ADE singularity→resolution graph\text{finite group}

\text{resolution graph}finite group→McKay graph→ADE singularity→resolution graph
This is a very strong graph–group–singularity triangle.
5. Quivers and singularities
A quiver is a directed graph. Quivers enter singularity theory through representation theory, moduli spaces, and ADE classifications.
Gabriel’s theorem says that quivers of finite representation type are exactly those whose underlying undirected graph is an ADE Dynkin diagram. MathOverflow
This connects:
directed graph→representation category→ADE classification→singularity geometry\text{directed graph}
\rightarrow
\text{representation category}

\text{singularity geometry}directed graph→representation category→ADE classification→singularity geometry
So quivers are another serious graph-theoretic doorway into singularity theory.
6. Graph hypersurfaces
There is also a more algebraic connection: from a finite graph Γ\GammaΓ, one can build a polynomial and a corresponding graph hypersurface. These hypersurfaces can have complicated singular loci.
Work on graph hypersurfaces says that the singular loci of graph hypersurfaces correspond set-theoretically to rank loci, and that the result depends on linear algebra. Intl Press
So in this direction:
graph→polynomial→hypersurface→singularities\text{graph}

\text{singularities}graph→polynomial→hypersurface→singularities
This is important in the algebraic geometry of Feynman integrals.

Pearl would be skeptical of transfer claims unless the graph has causal semantics.
He would probably say:
A graph is not enough. What are the causal variables? What are the interventions? What remains invariant under domain shift?

Readout
This experiment says:
Graph constraints are efficient when the classifier would otherwise waste capacity learning impossible transitions.
Typed features help when the scorer has enough context to use them.
Singularity flags are useful because low-margin states are much more failure-prone.
This was not a real BabyAI run and not the full hyperbolic architecture.
The clean takeaway:
The graph is load-bearing when it externalizes structure the model has not already learned.\boxed{
